THE PRAIRIE LEDGER  |  Science & Environment

Why a Small Town in Kansas Is Paying People to Tear Out Their Lawns

By Dana Whitfield
September 30th, 2026

HALSTEAD SPRINGS, Kan. - When Marvin and Lorraine Eckert dug up the
front lawn of their 1950s ranch house last spring, a neighbor asked
whether they were planning to sell. "He thought we'd given up," Lorraine
said, laughing, as she showed off a yard now full of purple coneflower,
little bluestem and butterfly milkweed. "Now he wants to know where we
got the seeds."

The Eckerts are among 214 households in Halstead Springs, population
6,800, that have joined the city's Prairie Yards rebate program since it
launched on April 1st, 2025. The program pays residents $1.50 per square
foot, up to $2,000, to replace irrigated turfgrass with native plants.

The motive is water. Halstead Springs draws almost all of its supply
from a shallow aquifer that has dropped by 11 feet over the past two
decades, according to the city's 2026 water master plan. During the
drought summer of 2023, outdoor irrigation accounted for nearly half of
the town's peak-day demand.

"We could keep drilling deeper wells, or we could stop pouring treated
drinking water on grass," said Reggie Tillman, the city's utilities
director. A new well field would cost an estimated $9.4 million; the
rebate program has spent $286,000 so far.

Early numbers are encouraging. A study by Dr. Anjali Mehra, a hydrologist
at Flint Hills State University, compared the water bills of
participating homes with those of similar homes nearby. Participants cut
their summer water use by an average of 38 percent. "The effect showed
up in the first summer, even before the plants were fully established,"
Mehra said. Her findings will be presented at a regional conference on
November 12th, 2026.

Native prairie plants, with root systems that can reach 10 to 15 feet,
survive Kansas summers with little or no watering once established.
They also support pollinators: volunteers from the local birding club
counted 23 butterfly species in converted yards this summer, against 6
in conventional lawns.

Not everyone is convinced. Some residents complained that the new yards
look "weedy," and the city had to amend its nuisance ordinance, which
previously required grass to be kept under 8 inches. Under the amended
rule, adopted in January, intentional native plantings are exempt if
they are set back two feet from the sidewalk and marked with a small
sign.

Applications for the 2027 round open on January 15th, 2027. The city
council will decide in its October budget hearings whether to expand
the program to commercial properties, starting with the strip of turf
around City Hall.

Dana Whitfield covers environment and agriculture for The Prairie Ledger.
